title: Hungary holds at 5.50% ahead of a reassessment of taxes and spending
summary: The November 17 Monetary Council maintained the base rate at 5.50% and the overnight corridor at 4.50–6.50%. October inflation was in line with September’s forecast, but a set of fiscal and regulatory measures complicated the outlook. Higher excise and other taxes and the removal of price-margin restrictions could raise measured prices, while cuts in government spending could moderate demand and inflation. The Council reserved a comprehensive assessment of their net impact for the December Inflation Report. It attached greater room for monetary policy to favourable domestic developments persisting and external uncertainty subsiding (rate table and concluding assessment).

October headline inflation rose to 2.0%, principally owing to fuel. Food prices remained below their levels a year earlier, and service inflation had changed little since August. Core inflation was 2.1%, with its monthly increase in line with the 2017–20 average. Household and company pricing expectations were moderate. These readings described an economy with subdued broad price momentum but renewed pressure in particular items. The 2.0% reading was at the lower edge of the existing tolerance band; the new 2.5% target was scheduled for January 2028 and should not be substituted for the current target in interpreting the meeting (price and mandate discussion).

The proposed inflation channels were unusually concrete. Removing margin restrictions could lift some retail prices. Higher excise on tobacco and spirits, the retail tax, the public health product tax and changes to the financial transaction tax could add to measured inflation. Their incidence depends on the extent and timing of pass-through, including whether retailers or banks absorb part of a levy. Lower public expenditure works differently, restraining aggregate demand over time. An unchanged nominal rate while the forecast is reassessed gives the Council time to distinguish a temporary tax-driven increase in the index from a broader change in inflationary pressure. The release gave no quantified net CPI impact of the package (policy measures and outlook).

Third-quarter GDP grew 1.5% year on year. Industry made the main positive contribution, services also supported growth and agriculture was a significant drag. September industrial production and retail sales both rose. Activity remained broadly in line with the September forecast. The Council identifies sector contributions but supplies no quarter-on-quarter comparison from which to infer a change in the pace of growth. For market interpretation, incoming tax and spending decisions could affect both domestic demand and investors’ assessment of the sovereign (activity and financial market assessments).

The interest-rate decision also had an exchange-rate channel. The Council argued that positive real interest rates and stable financial markets, particularly the foreign exchange market, help anchor inflation expectations. It noted that the ECB and Federal Reserve had held rates in October, even as market prices pointed to further tightening by major central banks during the year. In the region, Czech rates rose in November while Poland and Romania held. These are observed decisions and market expectations at the time. They help explain why a low domestic inflation print alone did not settle the case for a Hungarian cut.

Hungary’s domestic risk assessment had been stable for several months, helped by favourable reception of the fiscal path and the government’s commitment to euro adoption in its medium-term plan. Meanwhile global oil prices had fallen since October amid considerable volatility, European gas remained expensive and global technology-sector and political news weighed on risk appetite. The MNB described these as reasons for caution despite favourable domestic inflation. It gave no commitment to cut in December. The unchanged rates took effect on 18 November and the abridged minutes were scheduled for 2 December. These are distinct information dates for a currency or rates event study (external conditions and decision).

questions.question: When will higher taxes reach prices relative to the effect of spending cuts on demand?
questions.detail: The Council identifies channels pulling in opposite directions and gives no net CPI estimate. Build a calendar using enacted budget measures, tax guidance and the timetable for removing margin restrictions. Compare prices for affected goods with similar untaxed items and monitor actual public disbursements. The lag between the price and demand effects would change the timing of room for a rate cut.

questions.question: Was the low headline reading supported by broad disinflation?
questions.detail: Food was cheaper than a year earlier, fuel lifted headline inflation and monthly core momentum matched its 2017–20 average. Examine the statistical office’s monthly CPI components, price-change breadth and the MNB’s pricing-expectation surveys. Separate a one-off repricing of regulated items from repeated rises in unrelated services. The latter would make an early reduction in monetary restraint less likely.

questions.question: Is fiscal credibility doing enough to protect the forint and inflation expectations?
questions.detail: The release cites favourable market reception of the medium-term fiscal plan while identifying the exchange market as a policy constraint. Compare sovereign spreads, currency forwards, inflation compensation and household surveys around identifiable announcements, controlling for international yields and gas prices. A stronger currency-risk assessment can support local bonds even while new taxes raise the near-term consumer price index.
